title: Soft Pull vs. Hard Pull Credit Checks
seo_title: Soft Pull vs. Hard Pull Credit Checks | Fidelity Funding
meta_description: A soft pull does not affect your credit score; a hard pull can. Learn the difference, when each happens in business funding and how to protect your score.
dek: Not every credit check costs you points. Here is what separates a soft pull from a hard one and when each shows up in business funding.
intro: You want to explore your options for business funding, but you have worked hard on your credit and do not want to see a drop just for asking. It is a reasonable worry, and the answer depends on a distinction most people only learn when they need it: the difference between a soft credit pull and a hard one.

Both look at your credit file. They differ in why they happen, who sees them and whether they can move your score. Once you understand the two, you can shop for funding with far less anxiety and know what to expect at each stage.

paragraphs: A soft pull, or soft inquiry, is a review of your credit file that is not tied to a new credit application. It happens when you check your own report, when a lender pre-screens you for an offer, or when a company does a preliminary review with your permission. Soft pulls do not affect your credit score, and other lenders generally cannot see them when they review your report.

In business funding, a soft pull is often used for an initial assessment: confirming identity, getting a general sense of credit standing and deciding which options to explore. Fidelity Funding's process begins with a soft credit pull for the initial review, so starting a conversation does not put your score at risk.

A hard pull, or hard inquiry, occurs when you apply for credit and a lender checks your file to make a lending decision. Mortgage, auto and credit card applications are familiar examples. A hard inquiry is recorded on your report and can lower your score slightly, typically for a short period. The effect varies with your overall profile, and a single inquiry usually matters less than many.

Some business funding products, like larger term loans, SBA loans and certain lines of credit, involve a hard pull at the underwriting stage. Many short-term products rely mostly on bank statements and may use only soft inquiries. It depends on the funding partner and product, which is why you should ask.
The distinctions are easier to see in a list.
bullets: Soft pull: no score impact, not visible to other lenders, no application required
Hard pull: may reduce your score slightly, visible to others, tied to an application
Soft pull examples: checking your own report, prequalification, background checks
Hard pull examples: formal loan, line of credit or card applications
Both require appropriate authorization from you for business funding purposes

sections.h2: Why business owners get tripped up
paragraphs: Business funding often relies on the owner's personal credit, particularly for small companies, so a personal credit check can be part of the process even for business products. That is why the word "business" in the product name does not guarantee your personal score is untouched.

The other problem is applying in many places at once. Each formal application can generate its own hard inquiry. Models usually treat multiple inquiries of the same type within a short window as related shopping, but this is not universal, and not all credit products are treated identically. Submitting to ten unrelated lenders in a week is rarely a smart move. Working with a broker that starts with a soft pull and presents your profile to fitting partners cuts down the number of separate inquiries.

sections.h2: How to protect your score while exploring
paragraphs: A few habits keep your options open without paying for the privilege.
steps: Pull your own free credit reports first and correct any errors.
Ask every funder or broker whether the first review is a soft or hard inquiry.
Get a clear sense of the offers you would actually consider before authorizing a hard pull.
Keep formal applications for the products you are serious about, within a short window.
Avoid opening new personal credit during the process.
Note which inquiries you authorized, and dispute any you did not.

paragraphs: A few misconceptions cause needless worry. One is that any credit check lowers your score; soft pulls do not. Another is that checking your own report hurts you; it does not, and reviewing it before you apply is smart. A third is that a single hard inquiry will wreck your credit; for most people the effect is modest and fades, though many inquiries close together can add up. Finally, some owners assume that because a product is called a business loan, personal credit is irrelevant. Often it is not. When in doubt, ask the simple question: is this a soft or a hard inquiry, and will I be told before it happens?

sections.h2: What to expect from Fidelity Funding
paragraphs: The initial review uses a soft pull, and a funding specialist then walks you through options. If a particular partner or product requires a hard inquiry before final approval, your specialist should tell you at that stage so you can decide whether to move forward. You are never required to proceed. Credit is only one of several factors, along with deposits, time in business and existing obligations, so a less-than-perfect score does not automatically close doors. Ask questions about the credit check any time it is unclear.

key_takeaways: Soft pulls do not affect your score; hard pulls can lower it slightly.
Business funding may still involve your personal credit file.
Ask at every stage whether a credit check is soft or hard.
Avoid scattering formal applications across many lenders.
Fidelity Funding's initial review uses a soft pull.

faq.q: Does a soft credit pull hurt my score?
faq.a: No. Soft inquiries do not affect your credit score and are generally not visible to other lenders. They happen when you check your own report or when a company performs a preliminary review with your permission. Fidelity Funding begins with a soft pull for the initial review.

faq.q: How much does a hard inquiry lower my credit score?
faq.a: It varies with your credit profile, but the effect is usually small and temporary. People with long histories and few inquiries tend to see less change. A hard inquiry stays on your report for a period of time, so avoid unnecessary applications, especially close together.

faq.q: Do business loans check my personal credit?
faq.a: Often, yes, especially for small businesses where the owner personally guarantees the funding. Some products place more weight on business bank activity, while others rely heavily on personal credit. Ask your specialist how a given product treats it, and whether the check is soft or hard.

faq.q: Will shopping around with several lenders damage my credit?
faq.a: Multiple formal applications can create multiple hard inquiries. Scoring models sometimes group similar inquiries made in a short window, but treatment varies. Using a broker to review options through a single soft-pull process can reduce the number of separate inquiries you take on.

faq.q: When would a hard pull happen in a Fidelity Funding process?
faq.a: Only if a specific funding partner or product requires one before approval. Larger term products are more likely to than short-term ones. Your funding specialist should tell you beforehand so that you can decide whether to continue, and nothing is submitted without your authorization.
